x.ASV: For the Chief Musician; after the manner of Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. My soul waiteth in silence for God only: From him cometh my salvation.
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. On Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. UponGod alone doth my soul rest peacefully; from him is my salvation.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David. Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation.
x.YLT: To the Overseer, for Jeduthun. --A Psalm of David. Only--toward God is my soul silent, From Him is my salvation.

nt: David is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of waiting silently for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He is the one who saves me]

x.ASV: He only is my rock and my salvation: He is my high tower; I shall not be greatly moved.
x.Darby: He only is my rock and my salvation; my high fortress: I shall not be greatly moved.
x.KJV: He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
x.YLT: Only--He is my rock, and my salvation, My tower, I am not much moved.

nt: David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **rock** that provided stability and protection. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my foundation] or [my protector]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **stronghold**, a fortified place that protects people from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my place of safety] or [my protector]

The expression **I will not be greatly shaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nothing will shake me greatly] or [I will remain stable]

x.ASV: How long will ye set upon a man, That ye may slay him, all of you, Like a leaning wall, like a tottering fence?
x.Darby: How long will ye assail a man; will ye [seek], all of you, to break him down as a bowing wall or a tottering fence?
x.KJV: How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence.
x.YLT: Till when do ye devise mischief against a man? Ye are destroyed all of you, As a wall inclined, a hedge that is cast down.

nt: David is using the question form to express his frustration at his enemies for attacking him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have attacked me far too long!] or [Stop attacking me!]
Here the masculine term **a man** refers to the psalmist himself. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that makes this clear as modeled in the UST.

The expression **You will be smashed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will smash you] or [God will crush you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a leaning wall** and **an overthrown fence** will collapse, so the psalmist’s enemies will be destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and will collapse like a leaning wall or an overthrown fence]

x.ASV: They only consult to thrust him down from his dignity; They delight in lies; They bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. [Selah
x.Darby: They only consult to thrust [him] down from his excellency; they delight in lies; they bless with their mouth, but in their inward part they curse. Selah.
x.KJV: They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah.
x.YLT: Only--from his excellency They have consulted to drive away, They enjoy a lie, with their mouth they bless, And with their heart revile. Selah.

nt: The pronoun **him** refers to the psalmist. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to cast me down from my elevation]

The psalmist is speaking of the author’s honor and status as if it were **his elevation**, a high position from which he could be cast down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from his honored position] or [from his high status]

David is using one part of a person, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with their words] or [in their speech]

These two clauses, **with his mouth, they bless** and **in their inside, they curse**, mean basically opposite things. The psalmist is contrasting what his enemies say outwardly with what they feel inwardly. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition and contrast, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both clauses in your translation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the contrast more explicit. Alternate translation: [they say kind things, but they really wish harm]

Here, **inside** represents their hearts or inner thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their hearts] or [in their thoughts]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Pause and praise]

x.ASV: My soul, wait thou in silence for God only; For my expectation is from him.
x.Darby: UponGod alone, O my soul, rest peacefully; for my expectation is from him.
x.KJV: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
x.YLT: Only--for God, be silent, O my soul, For from Him is my hope.

nt: The psalmist is speaking to **his own soul** as if he were speaking to another person who could hear him. He is doing this to emphasize how strongly he feels about waiting for God alone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to himself or expressing his own determination. Alternate translation: [I shall be silent before God alone] or [I tell myself to wait quietly for God alone]

The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself in the act of waiting for God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I tell myself] or [self]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I await] or [what I confidently wait for]

x.ASV: He only is my rock and my salvation: He is my high tower; I shall not be moved.
x.Darby: He only is my rock and my salvation; my high fortress: I shall not be moved.
x.KJV: He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved.
x.YLT: Only--He is my rock and my salvation, My tower, I am not moved.

nt: David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **rock** and a **stronghold**, solid structures that could protect him from danger. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express these as comparisons. Alternate translation: [the one who protects me as would a rock and a stronghold]
If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nothing will shake me]

x.ASV: With God is my salvation and my glory: The rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.
x.Darby: WithGod is my salvation and my glory; the rock of my strength, my refuge is inGod.
x.KJV: In God is my salvation and my glory: the rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.
x.YLT: On God is my salvation, and my honour, The rock of my strength, my refuge is in God.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way, as modeled by the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what makes me honored]

David is speaking of God as if he were **the rock of** his **strength**, that is, a high rock that he could climb up to reach safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [God, who is like a rock that protects me and makes me strong] or [my strong protector]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the rock that strengthens me]

David is speaking of God as if he were a **refuge**, a place where he could go to be safe from danger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my place of safety] or [my place of protection]

x.ASV: Trust in him at all times, ye people; Pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. [Selah
x.Darby: Confide in him at all times, ye people; pour out your heart before him:God is our refuge. Selah.
x.KJV: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
x.YLT: Trust in Him at all times, O people, Pour forth before Him your heart, God is a refuge for us. Selah.

nt: The word translated as **Trust** is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation. Alternate translation: [I urge you to trust in him at all times, people]

The psalmist is using **Pour out your heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “express your emotions openly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Tell him honestly how you feel] or [Share your deepest emotions with him]
Here, **to his face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **a refuge**, a safe place to which people can go to escape danger. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is a safe place for us] or [is the one who protects us]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

x.ASV: Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: In the balances they will go up; They are together lighter than vanity.
x.Darby: Men of low degree are only vanity; men of high degree, a lie: laid in the balance, they go up together [lighter] than vanity.
x.KJV: Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.
x.YLT: Only--vanity are the low, a lie the high. In balances to go up they than vanity are lighter.

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [all people are vapor; indeed, they are a lie]

The psalmist is using **sons of a human** and **sons of a man** as common expressions of the culture to mean “people” or “human beings.” If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people … people] or [human beings … human beings]

The psalmist is speaking of people as if they were **vapor**. He means that people are transient and insubstantial. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are fleeting] or [have no substance]

When the psalmist says that people **are a lie**, he means that humans are deceptive in appearance and cannot be relied upon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are unreliable] or [are deceptive]

The psalmist says **they together would be lighter than vapor** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [together they would weigh almost nothing] or [all of them together have no weight at all]

x.ASV: Trust not in oppression, And become not vain in robbery: If riches increase, set not your heart thereon.
x.Darby: Put not confidence in oppression, and become not vain in robbery; if wealth increase, set not your heart upon it.
x.KJV: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.
x.YLT: Trust not in oppression, And in robbery become not vain, Wealth--when it increaseth--set not the heart.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in oppressing others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **robbery**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by robbing people] or [in what you rob from others]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Wealth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Should you become wealthy]

Here, **heart** represents a person’s desires and focus of attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [do not fix your desires on it] or [do not focus your attention on it]

x.ASV: God hath spoken once, Twice have I heard this, That power belongeth unto God.
x.Darby: Once hathGod spoken, twice have I heard this, that strength [belongeth] untoGod.
x.KJV: God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
x.YLT: Once hath God spoken, twice I heard this, That `strength is with God.'

nt: The psalmist is using **Once** and **twice** as a common expression to mean “repeatedly” or “with certainty.” The phrase emphasizes that God’s declaration is reliable and sure. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Repeatedly] or [Most certainly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God is powerful]

x.ASV: Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth lovingkindness; For thou renderest to every man according to his work.
x.Darby: And unto thee, O Lord, [belongeth] loving-kindness; for thou renderest to every man according to his work.
x.KJV: Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy: for thou renderest to every man according to his work.
x.YLT: And with Thee, O Lord, is kindness, For Thou dost recompense to each, According to his work!

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are faithful to your covenant] or [you are loyal and faithful]

The psalmist is repeating the pronoun **you** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that God is the one who repays. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you yourself repay] or [you alone repay]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to each person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **doing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to what he does]
